cues.text: Calculus studies how functions behave near inputs, so determine the real
domain
first.
A polynomial accepts every real input.
A rational function excludes zeros of its denominator.
A real square root requires a nonnegative argument, while a natural logarithm
requires a strictly positive argument.
For the quotient whose numerator is natural log of the quantity x minus one
and
whose denominator is x minus two, require x greater than one and exclude two.
The two conditions apply together.
Function sums and products use the common input domain; a quotient
additionally
excludes denominator zeros.
A composition requires the inner output to belong to the outer domain.
Simple graphs provide useful checks.
The square function is a parabola with nonnegative range.
The reciprocal function has separate branches and excludes zero.
The exponential e to the x is positive for every real x and has range all
positive reals.
Its inverse, natural log x, accepts positive inputs and has every real number
as a possible output.
Both are increasing.
Horizontal translations move excluded inputs as well as the visible graph.
Keep these restrictions through algebraic simplification and differentiation.
A derivative formula at an input outside the original function's domain does
not create a new valid point of that original function.
A limit describes values of a function as the input approaches a point through
nearby allowed inputs.
It does not require the function to be defined at the point itself.
For x squared minus four divided by x minus two, the expression equals x plus
two whenever x is not two.
As x approaches two from either side, the output approaches four.
The original expression still excludes x equal to two, so a limit value is not
an automatic point value.
Left and right limits inspect approaches from smaller and larger inputs.
A two sided finite limit exists only when both approaches give the same finite
number.
For x divided by absolute value of x near zero, the right hand values are one
and the left hand values are negative one.
The two sided limit therefore does not exist.
Defining any value at zero would not repair that jump in nearby behaviour.
Tables and graphs suggest limits but a finite collection of samples is not a
complete proof.
Algebra and standard limit laws justify the conclusions in the examples here.
An infinite limit describes unbounded behaviour rather than an ordinary real
output assigned at a singular input.
Direct substitution evaluates many limits of continuous elementary
expressions,
but zero divided by zero does not determine a value.
Factor common terms or use a conjugate while keeping the original exclusions.
For the quantity square root of one plus x, minus one, all divided by x,
substitution at zero gives this indeterminate form.
Multiply numerator and denominator by the quantity square root of one plus x,
plus one.
The numerator becomes x.
For nonzero x near zero, cancellation gives one divided by square root of one
plus x plus one, whose limit is one half.
The cancellation is justified near zero without defining the original quotient
at zero.
At infinity, compare leading powers.
For three x squared plus one divided by x squared minus two, divide numerator
and denominator by x squared.
The quotient becomes three plus one over x squared, divided by one minus two
over x squared, and tends to three as the input grows in magnitude.
Do not treat infinity as a number to substitute into ordinary arithmetic.
Each rewrite should preserve values on an appropriate nearby domain.
A simplification that changes one isolated point can still preserve the limit,
while changing values throughout a neighbourhood need not do so.
Several standard limits form the foundation of elementary differentiation.
With angles in radians, sine x divided by x tends to one as x tends to zero.
Replacing the angle by three x shows that sine three x divided by x tends to
three: multiply the standard sine ratio by three.
Using one minus cosine x equal to twice sine squared of x over two gives the
limit of one minus cosine x divided by x squared as one half.
Radian measure is essential for these numerical constants.
The exponential quotient e to the x minus one, divided by x, and the
logarithmic quotient natural log of one plus x divided by x both tend to one
near zero.
The logarithm requires one plus x positive, which is satisfied in a
sufficiently small neighbourhood of zero.
A related limit is one plus x raised to one over x tending to e, with positive
base and nonzero x near zero.
These standard limits may be established independently and then used to derive
derivative formulas.
Using those later derivative formulas as their only justification would be
circular.
Match the variable and scale carefully before applying a memorized form.
A function is continuous at an interior point a when its value exists, its two
sided limit exists, and that limit equals the value.
All three requirements matter.
Suppose f of x equals x squared minus one divided by x minus one for x not
equal to one, while f of one is a parameter k.
Nearby simplification gives x plus one, so the limit at one is two.
Continuity therefore requires k equal to two.
With that value the hole is filled consistently; any different value leaves a
point discontinuity.
Another example defines sine x divided by x away from zero and assigns c at
zero.
The standard limit is one, so continuity requires c equal to one.
A jump with unequal one sided limits cannot be fixed by choosing only one
point
value.
At an included endpoint of an interval, continuity is checked using the
approach available from inside the domain.
Polynomials are continuous throughout the reals.
Rational, logarithmic and other standard elementary expressions are continuous
where their relevant domain conditions are satisfied.
Use these facts to evaluate limits by substitution only after checking that
the
point belongs to the permitted domain and no exceptional piecewise boundary
has
been overlooked.
The derivative at an interior input x is the limit of f of x plus h minus f of
x, all divided by h, as nonzero h approaches zero.
The quotient measures the slope of a secant line.
Its limit, when finite and well defined, gives the instantaneous slope.
For f of x equal to x squared, expanding the numerator gives two x h plus h
squared.
Divide by h for nonzero h to obtain two x plus h; the limit is two x.
At x equal to three, the derivative is six.
Differentiability implies continuity: the function difference equals h times
the difference quotient, which tends to zero when the quotient has a finite
limit.
The converse fails.
Absolute value of x is continuous at zero, but its right difference quotient
there is one and its left quotient is negative one.
The derivative does not exist because those slopes disagree.
A corner is therefore different from a removable discontinuity.
At endpoints, one sided derivatives may be discussed separately, but they
should not be silently substituted for an ordinary two sided derivative.
Begin with the definition whenever a piecewise formula or a special point
makes
a standard rule uncertain.
For powers on their valid differentiable domains, the derivative of x to the
power n is n times x to the power n minus one.
Polynomial examples follow directly by differentiating each term.
Sums and differences differentiate term by term, and a constant multiple
remains a constant factor.
Products need both changing factors: the derivative of u v is u prime times v
plus u times v prime.
For x squared plus one multiplied by x minus one, the derivative is two x
times
x minus one plus x squared plus one, which simplifies to three x squared minus
two x plus one.
Multiplying the two derivatives alone would miss terms.
For a quotient u over v, use u prime v minus u v prime, divided by v squared,
with v nonzero.
Applying it to x divided by one plus x gives one divided by the square of one
plus x.
The original function excludes negative one, and the derivative formula does
too.
A constant exponent formula must also respect real domains when fractional or
negative exponents occur.
Check the type of operation before selecting the rule and retain the domain
alongside the result.
A composite function applies one operation after another.
The chain rule differentiates the outer function at the inner value and then
multiplies by the derivative of the inner function.
For sine of x squared, the outer derivative is cosine evaluated at x squared,
and the inner derivative is two x.
The result is two x cosine of x squared.
For three x plus one raised to the fifth power, the outer power rule gives
five
times that entire bracket raised to four.
The inner derivative three supplies another factor, giving fifteen times three
x plus one to the fourth.
Omitting the inner factor is a common error.
For a square root of one plus x squared, the derivative is one divided by
twice
that square root, multiplied by two x, giving x over square root of one plus x
squared.
Its denominator stays positive for every real x.
Several nested operations can be handled layer by layer, with each inner
derivative evaluated at the correct expression.
A derivative evaluated at an inner value is different from replacing the inner
function by its derivative inside the original outer function.
Keep brackets until all the chain factors have been written.
Radian measure gives the standard trigonometric derivative formulas.
Sine x differentiates to cosine x, and cosine x differentiates to negative
sine
x.
Applying the quotient rule to sine over cosine gives tangent's derivative as
secant squared x, where cosine is nonzero.
Cotangent differentiates to negative cosecant squared x where sine is nonzero.
For reciprocal functions, secant's derivative is secant x tangent x, and
cosecant's derivative is negative cosecant x cotangent x.
These formulas use the same domain restrictions as the original functions.
They do not assign derivatives at poles.
A scaled or composite angle needs the chain rule: sine of three x has
derivative three cosine three x, while tangent of x squared has derivative two
x secant squared of x squared at allowed inputs.
If the numerical input were measured in degrees rather than radians,
conversion
factors would enter the derivative.
State the angle convention before using a table of formulas.
The sine and cosine rules can be derived from the angle addition identities
and
the standard sine limit.
The remaining four then follow from quotient and reciprocal differentiation
rather than needing six unrelated memorized arguments.
Inverse derivative formulas follow by differentiating the corresponding direct
relation and respecting its branch.
For arcsine x, the derivative is one over square root of one minus x squared
for input strictly between negative one and one.
Arccosine has the negative of that derivative.
The inverse functions themselves accept the endpoints, but these finite
derivative formulas do not extend there.
Arctangent differentiates to one over one plus x squared for every real x.
Under our arccotangent convention, its derivative is negative one over one
plus
x squared.
For arcsecant, the derivative is one over absolute value of x times square
root
of x squared minus one.
Arccosecant has the negative of that expression.
Their derivative domains require absolute value of x greater than one.
The absolute value factor is important for negative inputs.
For arcsine of two x, the chain rule gives two over square root of one minus
four x squared, with derivative domain absolute value of x less than one half.
Distinguish the domain of an inverse function from the smaller set where its
ordinary finite derivative exists.
Our declared principal branches determine the signs consistently.
The exponential e to the x differentiates to itself, while natural log x has
derivative one over x on its positive domain.
For a constant positive base a, the derivative of a to the x is a to the x
times natural log a.
A logarithm to base a has derivative one divided by the product of x and
natural log a, with a positive and different from one and with x positive.
For natural log of two x plus one, the chain rule gives two over two x plus
one, and the original logarithm requires x greater than negative one half.
A variable power such as x to the x is not a constant exponent power rule
problem.
On x positive, set y equal to x to the x and take natural logs: natural log y
equals x natural log x.
Differentiating gives y prime over y equal to natural log x plus one.
Multiply back by y to obtain x to the x multiplied by the quantity natural log
x plus one.
Preserve the bracket around that final factor.
Taking logarithms requires the relevant positive quantities, so domain checks
come before the algebraic convenience of logarithmic differentiation.
An equation may define a curve without presenting y explicitly.
Differentiate both sides with respect to x and remember that y can depend on
x.
For x squared plus y squared equals twenty five, the result is two x plus two
y
times y prime equal to zero.
Where y is nonzero, solve to obtain y prime equal to negative x over y.
At the point three, four, the slope is negative three quarters, and a tangent
equation is y minus four equal to negative three quarters times x minus three.
Substituting the point into the original curve checks that the calculation is
being used at a valid location.
At five, zero, dividing by y is unavailable.
The circle nevertheless has a vertical tangent there, namely x equal to five.
One can verify the direction geometrically or differentiate x locally as a
function of y.
The ordinary finite slope dy over dx is absent at that point, which does not
mean the curve has no tangent line.
For more complicated relations, apply the chain rule to every expression
involving y and only then collect the y prime terms.
Keep the local solvability and denominator conditions with the result.
The second derivative measures the rate of change of the first derivative with
respect to the same variable.
For y equal to x cubed minus three x, the first derivative is three x squared
minus three and the second is six x.
Do not square the first derivative to obtain the second.
For a composite function, differentiate all the factors produced by the first
chain rule.
For implicit curves, the y expressions in a first derivative still depend on
x.
On the circle x squared plus y squared equals twenty five, the first
derivative
is negative x over y where y is nonzero.
A quotient rule differentiation gives negative of y minus x y prime, all
divided by y squared.
Replace y prime by negative x over y, then use x squared plus y squared equal
to twenty five.
The result is negative twenty five divided by y cubed.
At three, four, the second derivative is negative twenty five over sixty four.
This illustrates why holding y constant in the second differentiation would be
incorrect.
A second derivative can help classify a stationary point when its sign is
nonzero, but a zero second derivative alone gives no final classification.
We will combine it with sign tests and interval endpoints.
A derivative gives an instantaneous rate, while an average rate divides a
finite change in output by a finite change in input.
If displacement s of t is t cubed, instantaneous velocity is three t squared,
so at t equal to two it is twelve in the corresponding distance per time
units.
The average velocity over an interval generally differs.
For related rates, write a relation among the changing quantities before
differentiating.
A circle has area A equal to pi r squared.
If its radius changes with time, the chain rule gives d A over d t equal to
two
pi r times d r over d t.
At radius three centimetres and radial growth two centimetres per second, the
area grows at twelve pi square centimetres per second.
Substituting the fixed radius before differentiating would turn the area into
a
constant and lose the intended rate.
Differentiate the general relation first, then insert the instantaneous
values.
Units provide a useful check: a length times a length per second gives an area
per second.
State which rates are given, which rate is sought and the time or
configuration
at which they are evaluated.
The sign of a derivative describes local direction of change on an interval.
A positive derivative gives increasing behaviour, while a negative derivative
gives decreasing behaviour.
For f of x equal to x cubed minus three x, the derivative factors as three
times x minus one times x plus one.
Its zeros are negative one and one.
Test the three resulting open intervals.
The derivative is positive to the left of negative one, negative between
negative one and one, and positive to the right of one.
Thus f increases on the two outer intervals and decreases on the middle
interval.
A derivative equal to zero at one isolated point does not force a turning
point.
The function x cubed has zero derivative at zero but keeps increasing across
that point.
Also split at places where the derivative does not exist or the original
function is undefined; a sign table cannot silently join separate domain
components.
The endpoints of increasing or decreasing intervals need careful wording when
their inclusion is requested.
For solving inequalities, use the factored derivative signs rather than only a
rough sketch.
A graph can check the result, but the sign argument explains it across each
whole interval.
A local maximum occurs when nearby function values do not exceed the value at
the point; a local minimum reverses that comparison.
A derivative changing from positive to negative gives a local maximum, while
changing from negative to positive gives a local minimum.
For a stationary point, a negative second derivative gives a local maximum and
a positive second derivative gives a local minimum under the usual
differentiability conditions.
If the second derivative is zero, the test is inconclusive.
For example, x to the fourth has a minimum at zero while x cubed has neither a
maximum nor a minimum there, despite both having zero second derivative at
zero.
For absolute extrema on a closed bounded interval, compare every candidate and
the endpoints.
On zero through two, f equal to x cubed minus three x has an interior critical
point at one.
Its candidate values are f of zero equal to zero, f of one equal to negative
two, and f of two equal to two.
The absolute minimum is negative two at one and the maximum is two at the
endpoint two.
Checking only stationary points would miss that maximum.
A continuous function on a closed bounded interval attains its extremes; open
or unbounded intervals need separate existence checks.
